💡 Key Takeaways
  • The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) noted in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated.".
  • It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward.".
  • Shortly after Russia debuted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) noted in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated.".

It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward.".

Shortly after Russia debuted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS remarked that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence.".

Wednesday's statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.

Two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month, and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.

On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there.".

Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship.".

In a statement to DW on Wednesday, a German government spokesperson reiterated Berlin's position on the matter from the weekend, saying it viewed Friday's CAS ruling "very critically.".

The spokesperson also said  the government would "consult with the German Ice Hockey Federation in the near future regarding the potential consequences of this decision, including its impact on the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany.".

Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland, the defending men's world champions, has been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.

"We are at the moment working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson remarked.

This came shortly after Norway remarked it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

In a recent development, "Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.

Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.

Latvia's federation remarked it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.

Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia.".

USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.

Sources indicate that at the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades, told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.

"We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker noted.

Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.

On Wednesday afternoon, yet another sponsor joined the list, with German workwear company Strauss saying it would "forgo all logo exposure associated with the (men's) tournament" and was considering withdrawing its sponsporship entirely.

With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.

According to recent reports, this article was originally published on November 4, 2026. It was updated on November 5, 2026 with the German government statement to DW.

Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 91 min read (18232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~91 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics1,2.
  • Recent findings suggest that cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and is often considered to be an adaptive behaviour driven by ecological or social pressures1,2.
  • It has been revealed that locusts provide a compelling model for studies of cannibalism because of its crucial role in collective dynamics5,6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics1,2. Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented2, the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria, guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei. Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

Recent findings suggest that cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and is often considered to be an adaptive behaviour driven by ecological or social pressures1,2. However, its occurrence is highly context-dependent, and the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. In humans, cannibalism largely disappeared with cultural evolution, partly owing to prion diseases3. Similarly, insects such as crickets rarely engage in cannibalism under normal conditions, but confinement or nutritional deprivation can trigger this behaviour4. These observations highlight the influence of environmental pressures on cannibalism, although its intrinsic regulatory mechanisms remain unclear.

It has been revealed that locusts provide a compelling model for studies of cannibalism because of its crucial role in collective dynamics5,6. In juvenile migratory bands, the threat of conspecific predation from behind promotes forward movement, reducing cannibalistic risk and contributing to group cohesion5,6. Cannibalism also provides nutritional benefits, allowing locusts to compensate for food deficiencies and potentially enhancing survival and movement capacity7,8. This behaviour is strongly influenced by density-dependent phase polyphenism. At low densities, solitarious locusts avoid conspecifics, whereas increased population density promotes gregarious behaviour and cannibalistic encounters5,7. Nutritional deficiencies further exacerbate cannibalism. Field studies of South American locusts (Schistocerca cancellata) have demonstrated that carbohydrate deprivation promotes cannibalism9, whereas laboratory studies on desert locusts (Schistocerca gregaria) have shown that protein-biased diets reduce movement and increase cannibalistic interactions7. Although these findings establish the ecological importance of cannibalism, its molecular and genetic regulation remains poorly understood.

In a recent development, chemical cues regulate diverse locust behaviours, including aggregation10,11, oviposition12, mating13 and cannibalism14. Our previous work identified phenylacetonitrile (PAN) as a density-dependent anticannibalistic pheromone that activates specific olfactory receptors and reduces conspecific predation in crowded populations14. However, whether chemical cues actively induce cannibalism has remained unclear. Field and laboratory observations indicate that injured locusts are preferentially targeted by conspecifics15, suggesting that injury-induced chemical signals may attract individuals and promote cannibalistic behaviour.

In a recent development, guaiacol, a volatile compound produced by gut microbiota during plant digestion, has been identified as an aggregation pheromone in desert locusts16. Here we show that injury-induced microbiota-derived guaiacol coordinates immune defence and cannibalism in migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria) and elucidate the underlying mechanisms, which span microbial biosynthesis, olfactory detection, immune regulation and behavioural responses. Together, our findings identify a microbial signalling mechanism linking immunity and cannibalism, revealing how host–microbe interactions mediate a trade-off between immune protection and vulnerability to conspecific predation.

According to recent reports, cannibalism in L. migratoria exhibits phase polyphenism, with solitarious nymphs typically avoiding conspecific predation, whereas gregarious nymphs are more prone to engage in cannibalism, particularly under conditions of crowding or food scarcity14. Preliminary observations indicated that injured individuals were rapidly surrounded and attacked by nearby conspecifics (Fig. 1a), suggesting that injury itself serves as a cue that increases susceptibility to conspecific predation. To test this hypothesis, we conducted dual-choice assays with gregarious fourth- and fifth-instar nymphs, the developmental stages at which cannibalism is most prevalent14. As injury can alter locomotor performance and therefore influence predator choice independently of injury-derived signals, we controlled for this potentially confounding factor by immobilizing both prey individuals. This experimental design enabled us to specifically evaluate the contribution of injury-associated cues to predator preference. In each assay, pairs of immobilized intact and injured fourth-instar nymphs were presented at opposite ends of a chamber containing ten starved fifth-instar predators (Fig. 1b). Injuries were induced either mechanically or by previous conspecific bites. Across all assays, predators consistently exhibited a marked predation preference for injured over intact prey, indicating a significant role of injury in heightening vulnerability to conspecific predation (Fig. 1c).

a, Representative image of fifth-instar gregarious nymphs attacking an injured fourth-instar gregarious nymph. b, Schematic of the dual-choice predation assay. Ten starved fifth-instar gregarious nymphs were presented with one intact and one injured fourth-instar nymph immobilized at opposite ends of the arena. c–f, Predation preferences of intact (c; n = 15; group 1, P = 0.009; group 2, P = 0.012), ommatidectomized (d; n = 15; group 1, P = 0.001; group 2, P = 0.006), antennectomized (e; n = 15) and LmOrco−/− (f; n = 14) nymphs. Three prey pairings were tested: group 1, intact versus bitten; group 2, intact versus mechanically injured; group 3, mechanically injured versus bitten. g, Schematic of the dual-choice olfactometer assay testing volatiles from intact and injured fourth-instar nymphs. h,i, Olfactory preference of wild-type (h; n = 19; group 1, P = 0.010; group 2, P < 0.001) and LmOrco−/− (i; n = 15) nymphs for the three pairings described above. In c–f, preference is expressed as the percentage of total prey body mass consumed from each prey individual. All behavioural data are presented as box-and-whisker plots (boxes represent median and upper/lower quartiles; centre lines indicate the median, plus signs indicate the mean and whiskers extend from the minimum to the maximum values). Statistical analyses were performed using two-sided paired-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. ***P < 0.001; ** P < 0.01; * P < 0.05; NS, not significant.

According to recent reports, to determine whether the type of injury influenced predation preference, we compared predator preferences between mechanically injured and bitten prey. No significant difference was observed (Fig. 1c), indicating that injury alone, regardless of its origin, is sufficient to induce preferential predation. To explore whether injury-induced vulnerability was consistent across developmental stages, we extended the assays to first- to fifth-instar nymphs as prey. In all stages tested, fifth-instar predators consistently preferred injured prey over their intact counterparts, irrespective of injury type (Extended Data Fig. 1a). These findings demonstrate that injury-driven cannibalism is a robust and consistent trait across the development of gregarious locusts.

Recent findings suggest that next, we investigated the sensory cues mediating injury-induced predation. To assess the roles of olfactory and visual inputs, we performed antennal ablation (disrupting primary olfactory input), knocked out olfactory coreceptor LmOrco (disrupting olfactory receptor function) (Extended Data Fig. 1b) or removed the compound eyes (disrupting visual input). Predators with removed compound eyes retained their preference for injured prey (Fig. 1d), suggesting that visual cues are not required to mediate this behaviour. By contrast, predators lacking antennae or LmOrco function indicated no preference for injured over intact prey (Fig. 1e,f). Notably, although antennectomized predators no longer exhibited a statistically significant preference, a weak residual bias towards injured prey remained (Fig. 1e). This observation was consistent with the anatomical organization of the locust olfactory system, in which the antennae constitute the principal but not the exclusive olfactory organs. Consequently, antennal removal might substantially reduce but not completely eliminate olfactory perception. By contrast, disruption of LmOrco, which broadly impairs odorant receptor function, resulted in a complete loss of discriminatory behaviour (Fig. 1f). Together, these findings identify LmOrco-dependent olfaction as the primary sensory modality mediating injury-induced cannibalistic predation.

Finally, we assessed whether volatile chemical cues contributed to the observed predation bias. Headspace volatiles from both injured and intact nymphs were collected and presented in a dual-choice olfactometer (Fig. 1g). Starved fifth-instar predators strongly preferred the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals over the zone containing volatiles from intact prey (Fig. 1h). No significant difference in preference was observed between volatiles from mechanically versus bitten prey (Fig. 1h), indicating that injury-induced volatile release enhances predator attraction, thereby increasing the susceptibility of injured individuals to cannibalism. By contrast, LmOrco−/− predators showed no preference for the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals (Fig. 1i), indicating that LmOrco-dependent olfaction mediated the predation preference.

Industry observers note that to investigate the chemical signals underlying injury-induced cannibalism in L. migratoria, we analysed the headspace volatiles emitted by intact, mechanically injured and bitten locust nymphs (Fig. 2a). Among the compounds detected, guaiacol emerged as the dominant injury-affected odorant (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Table 1), with emission levels approximately ten-fold higher in injured nymphs compared with intact controls and gregarious adults (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This increase in guaiacol release was consistent across all developmental instars (first to fifth) (Extended Data Fig. 2c), suggesting that an increase in guaiacol production is a consistent physiological response to injury in gregarious nymphs. By contrast, other compounds—including PAN, which has previously been linked to suppression of cannibalism14—revealed no significant changes across injury conditions (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2d), indicating that guaiacol is a key injury cue.

According to recent reports, to assess the behavioural significance of guaiacol, we conducted dual-choice olfactometer assays with fifth-instar nymphs and male and female adults from both gregarious and solitarious phases, testing the effects of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Table 2) at a concentration of 10−3 (Fig. 2d). Only gregarious nymphs exhibited strong attraction to guaiacol; solitarious individuals and gregarious adults demonstrated no significant preference (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Video 1). This indicated that guaiacol selectively attracts gregarious nymphs. We then investigated whether the naturally emitted levels of guaiacol from injured gregarious nymphs were sufficient to trigger attraction. Quantitative headspace analysis showed that emissions from injured gregarious nymphs corresponded to concentrations equivalent to 10−5 to 10−4 dilutions of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2e). To determine whether these natural guaiacol emissions were sufficient to induce attraction, we tested behavioural responses of gregarious nymphs using a full concentration series (10−7 to 10−2) in a two-choice olfactometer (Fig. 2d). Attraction to guaiacol emerged sharply at 10−6 and remained robust at higher concentrations but disappeared at 10−7 (Fig. 2f). This aligned with the physiological range of natural emissions from injured nymphs, confirming that guaiacol concentrations released by injured individuals are behaviourally relevant. As all preceding behavioural assays were conducted with individually tested locusts, we next examined whether guaiacol attraction was preserved under the social conditions that characterize gregarious populations. To address this question, we performed dual-choice olfactometer assays using groups of five gregarious nymphs and quantified the average time spent by the group on each side of the arena. Consistent with the results obtained from individually tested animals, groups of gregarious nymphs spent significantly more time on the side containing 10−3 guaiacol than on the control side (Extended Data Fig. 2f and Supplementary Video 2). These findings demonstrate that the attractive effect of guaiacol persists in a group context and therefore probably operates under ecologically relevant social conditions.

As attraction alone does not necessarily imply a decision to engage in cannibalistic behaviour, we next investigated whether guaiacol could directly trigger cannibalistic predation. We performed two-choice predation assays, providing pairs of intact fourth-instar gregarious nymphs—one treated with 2 µl of 10−4 guaiacol (representing natural emission levels from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) and the other with solvent oil—to 10 starved fifth-instar gregarious predators (Fig. 2g). Guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially consumed, whereas solvent-treated nymphs were rarely attacked (Fig. 2h), confirming that guaiacol is a potent elicitor of cannibalistic predation. We then sought to rule out the potential influence of endogenous guaiacol on predator preference. Previous studies have shown that guaiacol is primarily synthesized by gut microbiota during plant digestion in locusts16. To eliminate this confounding factor, we generated germ-depleted gregarious nymphs by administering a cocktail of three antibiotics (tetracycline, streptomycin and ciprofloxacin) in their feed17,18,19 (Fig. 2i). This approach effectively abolished guaiacol emission in both intact and injured nymphs, providing a chemically clean background for subsequent behavioural assays (Fig. 2j). We then treated the germ-depleted gregarious nymphs with 2 µl of either 10−4 guaiacol (mimicking natural release from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) or solvent oil and used them as prey in dual-choice predation assays (Fig. 2i). As observed previously, guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially attacked, and solvent-treated nymphs were largely ignored (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 2g). Finally, to evaluate the ecological relevance of guaiacol-mediated cannibalism under more naturalistic conditions, we performed semi-field experiments in large outdoor mesh enclosures (1.8 m × 1.2 m × 1.5 m). Each enclosure contained 500 fifth-instar gregarious predators, together with 100 fourth-instar prey perfumed with either 10−4 guaiacol or solvent alone (Extended Data Fig. 2h). After 24 h, substantially fewer fourth-instar nymphs remained in guaiacol-treated enclosures than in control enclosures, indicating a significantly higher frequency of cannibalistic interactions in the presence of guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Consistent with direct behavioural observations, the reduction in surviving individuals was attributable to increased conspecific predation rather than escape, as all locusts were confined within the enclosure. These findings demonstrate that guaiacol-mediated promotion of cannibalism persists at the population level under seminatural conditions, supporting the ecological relevance of this injury-associated signal. Collectively, these findings establish guaiacol as a critical chemical cue that both signals injury and induces conspecific predation.

According to recent reports, to elucidate the molecular basis of guaiacol detection in L. migratoria, we sought to identify the specific olfactory receptors involved. In our previous study, we identified LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 as receptors responsive to guaiacol, on the basis of functional characterization of 49 L. migratoria olfactory receptors20. To confirm whether other olfactory receptors were involved in detection of this compound, we expanded our analysis to include a panel of 82 of approximately 140 identified L. migratoria olfactory receptors (Fig. 3a). Consistent with our earlier findings, LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 exhibited robust responses to guaiacol in a heterologous expression system (Fig. 3a,b), while no other receptor revealed comparable sensitivity.

It has been revealed that olfactory sensory neurons expressing different olfactory receptors are localized in distinct sensilla on the antennae of L. migratoria. To identify the sensilla responsible for guaiacol detection, we performed single-sensillum recordings (SSR) from basiconic and trichoid sensilla, which contain neurons expressing coreceptor Orco21,22. Basiconic sensilla harbour a larger population of sensory neurons (20–50), whereas trichoid sensilla contain only 2 or 3 neurons14. Owing to the higher neuronal density in basiconic sensilla, individual responses could not be distinguished on the basis of action potential amplitudes. Therefore, we measured the aggregate response of the entire neuronal population within the sensillum. Strong neuronal responses to guaiacol were detected in basiconic sensilla, whereas no response was observed in trichoid sensilla (Fig. 3c).

Inconsistent results were noted between electrophysiological and behavioural tests with respect to active concentrations of guaiacol, with a significantly higher threshold in the electrophysiological experiments. However, when we used solid-phase microextraction (SPME) technology to measure the concentration that actually reached the antenna during stimulation in the electrophysiological experiments, we found that the amount of guaiacol was comparable with the 10−6 dilution used in the behavioural assays (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

In a recent development, to assess the functional contribution of the LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 genes in vivo, we generated targeted loss-of-function mutants using CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing. Guide RNAs (Extended Data Table 3) targeting the first exon of these genes produced frame-shift deletions of 235 bp (LmOR34) (Extended Data Fig. 3b), 262 bp (LmOR36) (Extended Data Fig. 3b) and 8 bp (LmOR39) (Extended Data Fig. 3b), resulting in predicted truncations of the encoded proteins. Electroantennography (EAG) recordings demonstrated that the guaiacol-induced response was significantly reduced in LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants compared with wild-type nymphs, whereas the response in LmOR39−/− mutants remained unchanged (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, SSR recordings from basiconic sensilla demonstrated that neuronal response to guaiacol was significantly reduced in the LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants compared with wild-type nymphs, whereas LmOR39−/− locusts exhibited robust responses (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 3c). Taken together, these data indicate key roles of both LmOR34 and LmOR36 in mediation of the detection of guaiacol. We then investigated the behavioural consequences of these receptor disruptions. LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants showed a complete lack of attraction to guaiacol (Fig. 3f), in contrast to wild-type controls, which exhibited robust attraction. This loss of attraction was accompanied by a marked impairment in predation preference for guaiacol-treated prey nymphs (Fig. 3g). By contrast, the LmOR39−/− mutants showed no alteration in their behavioural and predation preferences (Fig. 3f,g), suggesting that LmOR34 and LmOR36 are essential for mediation of the behavioural response to guaiacol.

According to recent reports, our previous study showed that LmOR34 and LmOR36 also responded strongly to 2,4,6-trimethylpyridine (2,4,6-TMP)20 (Extended Data Fig. 3d), a compound that is highly attractive to gregarious locusts. To test whether this compound also promoted cannibalistic behaviour, we performed dual-choice predation assays (Extended Data Fig. 3e), presenting prey nymphs treated with either 2,4,6-TMP or solvent to starved gregarious predators. Predator nymphs showed no significant preference for 2,4,6-TMP-treated prey compared with controls (Extended Data Fig. 3e). These results showed that although 2,4,6-TMP is a potent attractant, it does not directly promote cannibalism, confirming that this compound has other ecological functions. To directly compare the effects of guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP on cannibalistic behaviour, we conducted a second dual-choice assay, in which prey nymphs were treated with either guaiacol or 2,4,6-TMP, both at a 10−4 dilution. Predator nymphs showed a strong preference for guaiacol-treated prey over 2,4,6-TMP-treated prey (Extended Data Fig. 3e). To further examine whether the observed predatory preference reflected a general response to behaviourally attractive locust volatiles, we performed a further dual-choice predation assay using 4-vinylanisole (4VA), another attractive locust odorant10. Predators were simultaneously offered two germ-depleted gregarious nymphs, one treated with 2 μl of a 10−4 dilution of guaiacol and the other with an equal volume of a 10−4 dilution of 4VA. Predator nymphs showed a significantly stronger preference for attacking and biting guaiacol-treated prey than 4VA-treated prey (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Together, these results demonstrate that enhanced predatory responses are not elicited by attractive locust volatiles in general but are specific to guaiacol, identifying guaiacol as a specialized chemical cue that promotes cannibalistic behaviour.

According to recent reports, notably, ligand-specific behavioural divergence despite shared receptor components has been widely documented across insects, including model species Drosophila melanogaster23,24, in which differential peripheral tuning25 and downstream circuit integration enable discrimination of chemically related cues26. To examine whether similar mechanisms operated in locusts, we compared the response properties of LmOR34 and LmOR36 to guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP. Although both ligands activated both receptors, guaiacol elicited markedly stronger and more sensitive responses than 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3f,g). Moreover, the response kinetics of LmOR34 and LmOR36 differed substantially between guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), indicating that these ligands impose distinct temporal activation patterns at the receptor level that could be differentially decoded by downstream circuits. In addition to receptor-intrinsic differences, ligand-specific behaviours are likely to be shaped by distinct population-level coding in the antennal lobe. Consistent with this idea, our previous study showed that the antennal lobe activation patterns evoked by guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP only partially overlapped27, suggesting other receptor inputs. For example, LmOR46 responds to 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3d), whereas LmOR39 responds to guaiacol (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, because only 82 of the 140 predicted L. migratoria olfactory receptors have been functionally characterized, other receptors may remain unidentified. Although these receptors may contribute only modestly to odour detection, even weak inputs could reshape ensemble coding in the antennal lobe, thereby biasing downstream circuit activation towards distinct ecological and behavioural outcomes. Together, differential receptor tuning (sensitivity and kinetics) and ligand-specific recruitment of other receptors probably explain why guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP produce divergent behavioural consequences despite engaging shared receptors.

Guaiacol has previously been identified as a volatile produced by Pantoea agglomerans in the gut of S. gregaria and has been implicated in locust behaviour16. To identify guaiacol-producing bacteria in L. migratoria, we performed gut microbiota metagenomic sequencing but did not detect P. agglomerans (Fig. 4a), suggesting alternative microbial sources. We subsequently isolated cultivable bacteria from the gut and haemolymph of fourth-instar gregarious nymphs (Fig. 4b). Screening of more than 50 colonies identified a guaiacol-producing isolate from both tissues (Fig. 4b,c), which whole-genome sequencing identified as Enterobacter hormaechei, a dominant gut bacterium (Fig. 4a). Metagenomic analyses further confirmed high abundance of this bacterium in both the gut and haemolymph (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Although E. hormaechei was not reported in a previous study of the L. migratoria microbiome28, metagenomic sequencing and quantitative PCR (qPCR) detected it in all six geographically distinct field populations examined, with varying relative abundances (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Screening of other isolates also identified Klebsiella pneumoniae as a guaiacol producer, with emission levels comparable with those of E. hormaechei (Fig. 4c). However, we selected E. hormaechei for subsequent mechanistic analyses as it was consistently detected across samples and populations and exhibited stable guaiacol production.

Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used, except in f (Pearson correlation). Independent individuals were used at each time point in d–f. Haemolymph (approximately 5 μl per locust) was pooled from 20 individuals per biological replicate. ***P < 0.001; **P < 0.01; *P < 0.05.

We next examined the relationships of injury with bacterial abundance and guaiacol emission. Following injury, both haemolymph bacterial loads (Fig. 4d) and guaiacol emission (Fig. 4e) increased over time, peaking approximately 6 h after injury and stabilizing at around 8 h (Fig. 4d,e), and their temporal changes were positively correlated (Fig. 4f). To assess localized bacterial enrichment, we collected equal volumes of haemolymph from wound sites and intact regions of the same individuals 6 h after injury (Fig. 4g). Wound-site haemolymph had significantly higher bacterial loads (Fig. 4h) and guaiacol levels (Fig. 4i), indicating localized accumulation of E. hormaechei and enhanced guaiacol production. As population density can influence locust gut microbiota29, we also compared E. hormaechei abundance between phases and found no significant difference between solitarious and gregarious nymphs (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

Industry observers note that to determine whether E. hormaechei influenced locust behaviour, we first tested its volatiles in a two-choice olfactometer (Fig. 4j). Gregarious nymphs were significantly attracted to bacterial volatiles relative to the control medium (Fig. 4k). We then examined whether these volatiles promoted cannibalism using dual-choice predation assays (Fig. 4l). Two mechanically injured germ-depleted prey nymphs, matched for injury size and location, were presented simultaneously to ten starved fifth-instar gregarious predators, with one prey recolonized with E. hormaechei and the other left untreated. Predators preferentially attacked and consumed prey harbouring E. hormaechei, whereas germ-depleted controls were rarely targeted (Fig. 4m).

To identify the genetic basis of guaiacol biosynthesis, we sequenced the E. hormaechei genome and identified a cluster of three vanillic acid decarboxylase (vdc) genes, which have been previously implicated in microbial conversion of vanillic acid to guaiacol30 (Fig. 4n). Heterologous expression of this cluster in Escherichia coli (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 1) confirmed its capacity to catalyse guaiacol production from vanillic acid in vitro (Fig. 4o). Conversely, deletion of the vdc genes in E. hormaechei (Extended Data Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 1) completely abolished guaiacol production, as confirmed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) (Fig. 4p). These findings establish an essential role of this gene cluster in guaiacol biosynthesis.

Finally, we assessed whether microbial guaiacol biosynthesis was required for locust attraction and cannibalism. In two-choice olfactometer assays, gregarious nymphs were attracted to volatiles from wild-type E. hormaechei but not vdc-deficient mutants (Fig. 4q). Similarly, in dual-choice predation assays, starved gregarious predators preferentially attacked mechanically injured germ-depleted prey recolonized with wild-type E. hormaechei, whereas prey harbouring vdc mutants were rarely targeted despite identical injury size and location (Fig. 4r). Together, these results demonstrate that injury-associated guaiacol production by E. hormaechei is essential for converting host injury into an olfactory cue that promotes conspecific attraction and cannibalism.

According to recent reports, injured gregarious nymphs release elevated levels of guaiacol despite the increased risk of conspecific cannibalism. This raises the question of why such a seemingly costly response is maintained. We considered that guaiacol release might provide compensatory benefits to injured individuals. To explore this possibility, we first considered the antimicrobial properties of guaiacol. Previous studies have shown that guaiacol can inhibit or kill a broad range of microorganisms, including bacteria and fungi; these activities were attributed to its phenolic structure, which disrupts microbial membranes and interferes with metabolic processes31,32,33. On the basis of these properties, we proposed that guaiacol produced by E. hormaechei could provide immune benefits to injured gregarious nymphs by suppressing pathogen invasion.

Recent findings suggest that to test this hypothesis, we selected two pathogens commonly associated with locust mortality: intrinsic locust bacterial pathogen Proteus mirabilis34 (Extended Data Fig. 5a) and commercially available fungal insecticide Metarhizium anisopliae35 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). To determine whether guaiacol could improve resistance to pathogen invasion following injury, we used germ-depleted gregarious nymphs, which were either fed guaiacol or left untreated, and infected them with either wild-type E. hormaechei or its vdc knockout mutant (Fig. 5a). After manually injuring the nymphs, we applied infections with both M. anisopliae and P. mirabilis to the wound sites and monitored survival over several days (Fig. 5a). We found that guaiacol-fed or wild-type E. hormaechei-infected nymphs exhibited significantly higher survival rates compared with those that were non-fed or infected with the vdc-mutant E. hormaechei (Fig. 5b,c). These results indicated that guaiacol, produced by E. hormaechei, might enhance the survival of injured nymphs when exposed to pathogen infection. To confirm that this protective effect was due to the ability of guaiacol to inhibit pathogen proliferation, we quantified pathogen loads in the haemolymph of guaiacol-fed and non-fed nymphs, as well as in those infected with wild-type or vdc-mutant E. hormaechei. We observed that pathogen burdens were significantly higher in the haemolymph of non-fed and vdc-mutant-infected nymphs compared with guaiacol-fed and wild-type E. hormaechei-infected nymphs (Fig. 5d,e). These findings support the notion that guaiacol production by E. hormaechei suppresses invasion and proliferation of M. anisopliae and P. mirabilis, thereby providing immune benefits to injured locusts. Finally, to determine whether the protective effect of guaiacol-producing E. hormaechei was pathogen-specific or broadly applicable, we infected injured locusts with another opportunistic pathogen, Enterococcus faecalis34 (Extended Data Fig. 5c). As observed for P. mirabilis and M. anisopliae, guaiacol supplementation and colonization by wild-type E. hormaechei significantly suppressed pathogen infection (Extended Data Fig. 5d) and enhanced host survival (Extended Data Fig. 5e). Together, these results indicate that guaiacol functions as a broadly protective microbial metabolite that enhances host defence against diverse pathogens following injury.

PBS, phosphate-buffered saline. g, Functional annotation of differentially expressed genes; four Toll and Imd pathway genes are highlighted. h, Relative mRNA levels after guaiacol treatment (n = 3): LBP (3 h, 6 h, 9 h; P = 0.002, P = 0.004, P < 0.001), βGBP (6 h, 9 h; P = 0.030, P = 0.042), PGRP-SD (3 h, 6 h, 9 h; P = 0.003, P < 0.001, P = 0.014) and CatL (6 h, 9 h; P = 0.007, P < 0.001). i, RNAi workflow. j–l, Survival after knockdown of LBP (j; n = 80, P = 0.007), CatL (k; n = 100, P = 0.019) or βGBP (l; n = 80, P < 0.001) versus GFP controls. m, Workflow assessing immune benefits to predators consuming E. hormaechei-carrying prey. n,o, Predator survival after consumption of germ-depleted or E. hormaechei (E. h)-infected prey, followed by P. mirabilis (n; n = 100, P = 0.001) or M. anisopliae (o; n = 120, P < 0.001) infection. Data are mean ± s.d. (d, e and h). Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-tests were used, except in survival analyses (b, c, j–l, n, o; log-rank Mantel–Cox tests). ***P < 0.001; **P < 0.01; *P < 0.05. The dsGFP data presented in panels j and k are identical, as both originate from the same experiment.

To explore the mechanism underlying the suppression of pathogen proliferation, we first tested whether guaiacol directly inhibited the growth of M. anisopliae and P. mirabilis in vitro using the inhibition zone method. However, we found that both purified guaiacol and E. hormaechei failed to inhibit the growth of either pathogen (Extended Data Fig. 5f), suggesting that guaiacol does not directly suppress pathogen growth in vitro. Given this background, we proposed that the suppression of pathogen proliferation by guaiacol might instead be linked to an altered immune response in the locusts that confers enhanced pathogen resistance. In locusts, the haemolymph plays a critical part in immune defence36. To investigate the involvement of guaiacol in immune response regulation, we sequenced the transcriptomes of the haemolymph at the wound site from guaiacol-fed and non-fed germ-depleted gregarious nymphs after 3 h, 6 h and 9 h of injury (Fig. 5f). Differential gene expression analysis showed that substantial numbers of genes were upregulated and downregulated in the guaiacol-fed nymphs compared with the non-fed nymphs. Notably, four upregulated genes were identified in the Toll and Imd signalling pathways (Fig. 5g,h), which are known to be involved in immune defence37,38,39,40,41,42,43. These four genes, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) and cathepsin L (CatL) have been shown to resist Gram-negative bacterial infections37,38,39, whereas β-glucan-binding protein (βGBP) has been associated with resistance to fungal infections in several insect species40,41. We proposed that in locusts, LBP and CatL might help to resist P. mirabilis infection, whereas βGBP might protect against M. anisopliae infection.

Recent findings suggest that to validate the roles of these genes in pathogen resistance, we used RNA interference (RNAi) (Fig. 5i) to knock down each gene individually (Extended Data Fig. 5g-i) and assessed their contributions to resistance to M. anisopliae or P. mirabilis infections. We found that knockdown of LBP and CatL (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h) promoted the invasion and proliferation of P. mirabilis (Extended Data Fig. 5j,k), leading to significantly higher mortality compared with the control GFP RNAi group (Fig. 5j,k). Knockdown of βGBP (Extended Data Fig. 5i), on the other hand, facilitated the invasion and proliferation of M. anisopliae (Extended Data Fig. 5l), also resulting in significantly higher mortality compared with the GFP RNAi control (Fig. 5l). These results indicate that guaiacol enhances resistance to P. mirabilis infection by upregulating LBP and CatL, while enhancing resistance to M. anisopliae through upregulation of βGBP. Thus, guaiacol protects injured nymphs from pathogen infection by stimulating the immune response.

As guaiacol activated immune responses in injured locusts, we next asked whether this immune activation might also restrict the proliferation of the guaiacol-producing symbiont itself. To address this possibility, we exposed germ-depleted gregarious nymphs to guaiacol or left them untreated and subsequently inoculated them with equal amounts of E. hormaechei. Under these conditions, guaiacol exposure did not reduce E. hormaechei abundance relative to untreated controls (Extended Data Fig. 5m), indicating that guaiacol-induced immune activation does not substantially impair colonization by its microbial producer. We then examined whether elevated guaiacol emission served as a direct consequence of pathogen infection. Gregarious nymphs were infected with P. mirabilis, and guaiacol emission was quantified following infection. Pathogen infection alone did not significantly alter guaiacol release compared with uninfected controls (Extended Data Fig. 5n), suggesting that elevated guaiacol production is not a general response to infection but instead is specifically associated with injury-dependent proliferation of E. hormaechei.

Recent findings suggest that having established that guaiacol neither suppresses its microbial producer nor is directly induced by pathogen infection, we next asked whether guaiacol exposure enhanced the capacity of the host to respond to subsequent pathogen challenge. Germ-depleted gregarious nymphs were fed guaiacol before localized infection of a wound site with P. mirabilis. Guaiacol treatment resulted in upregulation of multiple genes in the Toll and Imd signalling pathways, including the immune effector genes identified earlier (Extended Data Fig. 5o). These results indicate that guaiacol may enhance host immune responsiveness during subsequent bacterial infection.

Sources indicate that finally, we explored whether gregarious predator nymphs benefited from consuming injured gregarious nymphs, given that these injured nymphs host large quantities of E. hormaechei. In the experimental group, we provided germ-depleted fourth-instar gregarious nymphs infected with E. hormaechei to fifth-instar gregarious predator nymphs for feeding (Fig. 5m). In the control group, we provided germ-depleted fourth-instar gregarious nymphs without E. hormaechei infection (Fig. 5m). In both groups, we ensured that all predator nymphs consumed equal amounts of prey nymphs. We found that predators consuming E. hormaechei-infected nymphs exhibited significantly better survival when subsequently infected with pathogens, compared with those that consumed non-infected nymphs (Fig. 5n,o). To directly trace microbial transmission during cannibalism, we fed germ-depleted fifth-instar predator nymphs with prey carrying E. hormaechei (Extended Data Fig. 5p). Several days after feeding, large quantities of E. hormaechei were detected throughout the haemolymph of predator nymphs, and this was accompanied by guaiacol production (Extended Data Fig. 5q,r). By contrast, predators fed prey lacking bacteria exhibited neither E. hormaechei loads nor measurable guaiacol emission (Extended Data Fig. 5q,r). These findings demonstrate that E. hormaechei acquired through cannibalism can successfully establish in the predator haemolymph and retain its metabolic capacity to produce guaiacol following transmission.

Together, these results indicate that predator locusts may derive benefits from consuming injured nymphs, probably owing to microbial and immune support provided by the accumulated E. hormaechei.

Sources indicate that our findings demonstrate that guaiacol functions as both an internal and an external signal in gregarious locusts, acting internally to enhance immune defence while externally promoting cannibalism. This dual role probably represents an evolutionary adaptation that balances pathogen resistance with the risks of conspecific predation in response to fluctuating physiological conditions, such as injury severity. To investigate how injury severity influenced these opposing effects, we generated standardized injuries of increasing size (levels 1–6) using steel needles (Fig. 6a and Extended Data Fig. 6a). Guaiacol emissions remained low at injury levels 1–3 but increased significantly at levels 4–6 (Fig. 6b). Consistent with this pattern, starved gregarious predators demonstrated no preference between intact and injured prey at levels 1–3 but preferentially attacked injured nymphs at levels 4–6 (Fig. 6a,c). The latter injuries approximated those caused by hind-tarsus loss or bites from fifth-instar locusts (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Prey movement distance and speed did not differ significantly across injury levels (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c); this enabled us to exclude differences in mobility as an explanation for predation preferences. These results indicate that elevated guaiacol emission associated with severe injury promotes cannibalistic attacks.
